entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5187"/><div sID="gen7724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5187"/><hi type="bold">8. thy words--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.17">16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.5">27:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.14">29:14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Job.9.30">Job 9:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.23">13:23</reference>, Job had acknowledged sin; but the general spirit of his words was to maintain himself to be "clean," and to charge God with injustice. He went too far on the opposite side in opposing the friends' false charge of hypocrisy. Even the godly, though willing to confess themselves sinners in general, often dislike sin in particular to be brought as a charge against them. Affliction is therefore needed to bring them to feel that sin in them deserves even worse than they suffer and that God does them no injustice. Then at last humbled under God they find, affliction is for their real good, and so at last it is taken away either here, or at least at death. To teach this is Elihu's mission. <div eID="gen7724" type="x-p"/>

entries.reader_content_plain: 22. destroyers-- angels of death commissioned by God to end man's life ( 2Sa 24:16 ; Psa 78:49 ). The death pains personified may, however, be meant; so "gnawers" (see on Job 30:17 ).

Elihu refers to himself as the divinely-sent (<reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">33:6</reference>) "messenger," the "interpreter" to explain to Job and vindicate God's righteousness; such a one Eliphaz had denied that Job could look for (<reference osisRef="Job.5.1">Job 5:1</reference>), and Job (<reference osisRef="Job.9.33">Job 9:33</reference>) had wished for such a "daysman" or umpire between him and God. The "messenger" of good is antithetical to the "destroyers" (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>).<div eID="gen7746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with him--</hi>if there be vouchsafed to the sufferer. The office of the interpreter is stated "to show unto man God's uprightness" in His dealings; or, as Umbreit, "man's upright course towards God" (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.2">Pr 14:2</reference>). The former is better; Job maintained his own "uprightness" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.17">Job 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.5">27:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.6">6</reference>); Elihu on the contrary maintains God's, and that man's true uprightness lies in submission to God. "One among a thousand" is a man rarely to be found. So Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>). Elihu, the God-sent mediator of a temporal deliverance, is a type of the God-man Jesus Christ the Mediator of eternal deliverance: "the messenger of the covenant" (Mal 3:1). This is the wonderful work of the Holy Ghost, that persons and events move in their own sphere in such a way as unconsciously to shadow forth Him, whose "testimony is the Spirit of prophecy"; as the same point may be center of a small and of a vastly larger concentric circle. <div eID="gen7747" type="x-p"/>

Apodosis to <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>.<div eID="gen7748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God.<div eID="gen7749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Deliver--</hi>literally, "redeem"; in it and "ransom" there is reference to the consideration, on account of which God pardons and relieves the sufferers; here it is primarily the intercession of Elihu. But the language is too strong for its full meaning to be exhausted by this. The Holy Ghost has suggested language which receives its full realization only in the "eternal redemption found" by God in the price paid by Jesus Christ for it; that is, His blood and meritorious intercession (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>). "Obtained," literally, "found"; implying the earnest zeal, wisdom, and faithfulness of the finder, and the newness and joyousness of the finding. Jesus Christ could not but have found it, but still His seeking it was needed [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.8">Lu 15:8</reference>). God the Father, is the Finder (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">Psa 89:19</reference>). Jesus Christ the Redeemer, to whom He saith, Redeem (so Hebrew) him from going, &c. (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen7750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ransom--</hi>used in a general sense by Elihu, but meant by the Holy Ghost in its strict sense as applied to Jesus Christ, of a price paid for deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.30">Ex 21:30</reference>), an atonement (that is, means of selling at once, that is, reconciling "two" who are estranged), a covering, as of the ark with pitch, typical of what covers us sinners from wrath (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.14">Ge 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>). The pit is primarily here the grave (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Is 38:17</reference>), but the spiritual pit is mainly shadowed forth (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">Zec 9:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7751" type="x-p"/>

Effects of restoration to God's favor; literally, to Job a temporal revival; spiritually, an eternal regeneration. The striking words cannot be restricted to their temporal meaning, as used by Elihu (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen7752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his flesh shall be fresher than a child's--</hi>so Naaman, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.14">2Ki 5:14</reference>, spiritually, <reference osisRef="John.3.3-John.3.7">Joh 3:3-7</reference>. <div eID="gen7753" type="x-p"/>
